In this study, we introduce a novel backdoor attack called "Clean-to-Clean" (C2C) that enables triggers to be embedded in plain sight, without affecting the model's performance on benign data. C2C attacks are characterized by their ability to function normally with clean data, fail with triggered data, and maintain performance on data with random corruption, making it difficult to detect. Our experiments on multiple datasets and architectures demonstrate the effectiveness of C2C attacks, which can be transferred to various pre-trained models with high success rates. Furthermore, we propose a detection method that can identify C2C attacks with high accuracy, even when the trigger is unknown, by utilizing random corruption and synthetic data. Our research highlights the need for developing robust DNNs that can withstand various types of attacks, including C2C attacks, to ensure their safe deployment in real-world applications. The field of concept learning has garnered significant attention, yet most research focuses on the individual level, ignoring the transfer of concepts to other domains.  We propose an innovative approach to concept learning, where a model learns to extract high-level concepts from images and transfers these concepts to novel image sets.  Our framework, Image Concept Learning with Image Generation, integrates two tasks: image generation and image reconstruction.  The image generation task creates diverse images that expose the concept embeddings to varying patterns, whereas the image reconstruction task reconstructs concept embeddings from input images, ensuring their consistency across various image sets.  We evaluate our approach on the ImageNet dataset and demonstrate its ability to extract meaningful concepts from images and transfer them to novel image sets.  The results show that our approach outperforms existing methods in concept learning and can effectively transfer learned concepts to novel image sets.  The code and models are publicly available at https://github.com/linweee/I-CLIG. Current surveillance systems heavily rely on manual reporting by healthcare professionals.
This approach has significant limitations, making it inadequate for timely detection of rare or unfamiliar pathogens. To address these issues, researchers have developed methods for extracting infectious disease data from unstructured sources. However, these methods require significant manual annotation and labeling, which can be labor-intensive and costly. In contrast, our proposed system leverages the capabilities of pre-trained language models for automated disease surveillance. Our approach involves training a transformer-based model on various sources of unstructured text data, including scientific literature and news articles. This training enables the model to learn disease-related information and identify patterns indicative of outbreaks. Our evaluation on a dataset of established outbreaks demonstrates the system's ability to detect disease-related text at an early stage, even before official reports are published. This capability allows for the generation of early alerts and early warning systems. When applied to a diverse set of unlinked text from 2019, our system achieved a high F1 score of 0.89 in detecting SARS-CoV-2-related text from multiple sources. This performance is comparable to or even superior to existing state-of-the-art models. Our proposed system has the potential to be a game-changer in infectious disease surveillance. To facilitate further research, we have made our model and training code publicly available. This open access will enable the model to be fine-tuned for specific applications and enhance its utility for disease surveillance. To facilitate this, we have created a user-friendly web interface to allow users to input unstructured text and generate early alerts and estimate the timing of outbreaks. Our system has the potential to be a valuable resource for public health professionals and researchers in related fields. types are randomly sampled, which often leads to biased representation of error types. To address this limitation, we introduce a new metric, the Expected Error Type Specificity (EEST). This metric estimates the likelihood that the test data accurately represents the error types present in the evaluation metrics. To calculate EEST, we first determine the frequency of each error type in the training data and then assess its representation in the test data. EEST is calculated as the standard deviation of the error type distribution, which ranges from 0 to infinity. Our analysis reveals that the test data marginally underrepresents error types. However, the data overrepresents specific error types, which are less frequent but more prevalent in the test data. EEST is utilized to calculate a weighting factor for each error type to adjust the standard evaluation metrics. Through an experiment on a large-scale dataset, we demonstrate that the weighted evaluation metrics exhibit reduced variability in scores compared to the standard metrics. This adjustment also results in more discerning system rankings. Furthermore, we find that the top-performing systems exhibit a notable decline in performance when evaluated on the test set with the adjusted weighting. Our study contributes to the field by introducing EEST, providing a more nuanced understanding of error type representation in test data and offering a method to adjust evaluation metrics accordingly. Traditional approaches to image restoration struggle to effectively handle these complexities. To address this issue, we introduce a novel two-stage image restoration framework that first generates a clear background image and then accurately restores the original content. Our method achieves this by learning the underlying relationships between images using a graph structure that represents their inherent properties. In the first stage, we utilize a graph learning approach to infer the background image from a background model, which we construct by analyzing the commonalities of image patches. The clear background image we obtain is then used to guide the second stage of the restoration process. To refine the restored image, we employ a conditional adversarial network that leverages both the background image and the input patch to predict the original content. Our proposed framework is evaluated on a range of dynamic image restoration tasks, including deblurring, deringing, and defocus deblurring, and outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in terms of both quantitative and qualitative metrics. This Galois correspondence equates closed maps between tropical curves that preserve divisors with their corresponding automorphisms, subject to a Galois action restriction. The Galois mapping characteristic can be viewed as a Galois correspondence analogue between the tangent bundle of a tropical curve and its derivative, each associated with a natural group action. Our findings imply that every tropical curve has a unique tangent bundle Galois extension, and this extension's tangent bundle is the derivative of the extended curve. Moreover, we show that tropical curves are a type of tropical variety with a Henselian residue field, and we establish a Galois correspondence for unramified coverings between tropical varieties and open immersions that preserve regularity.
